lesson.title: The Would-World
lesson.subtitle: je voudrais, tu pourrais, je ferais — the conditional politeness escalator and the -ai future tense

hook.title: How Future Stem + Imparfait Ending Creates 'Would'
hook.content: What is 'would' historically? In English, 'would' is literally the past tense of 'will' ('I wished that I would...'). French builds its Would-World (le conditionnel) using the exact same recipe! It takes the future stem (always ending in the sound /ʁ/) and welds on the -ais/-ait endings from the imparfait (Topic 19): vouloir → je voudrais ('I would like'), pouvoir → tu pourrais ('you could'), faire → je ferais ('I would do/make'), parler → je parlerais ('I would speak').

footnotes.title: Why the French future tense is literally Infinitive + J'ai
footnotes.content: Vulgar Latin formed the future by gluing habēre ('to have') onto the back of the infinitive: parler + ai ('I have to speak') → je parlerai ('I will speak'), parler + as → tu parleras, parler + a → il parlera!

pattern.title: The Politeness Escalator: je veux → je voudrais
pattern.content: In Topic 1 you learned je veux ('I want'). In a Paris bistro or shop, saying Je veux un café sounds blunt — like banging on the counter. Step onto the conditional escalator and say Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît ('I would like a coffee, please') or Tu pourrais m'aider ? ('Could you help me?'). And just like je veux, je voudrais chains directly with any bare infinitive: Je voudrais réserver une table ('I would like to reserve a table').
pattern.linguist_note: Both the synthetic future (-ai, -as, -a) and conditional (-ais, -ais, -ait) are Medieval Romance fusions of the infinitive + present/imperfect of habēre.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: using blunt Je veux when ordering in a restaurant or shop. Step up to the conditional Je voudrais for polite requests!

exercises.prompt: Match each conditional or future form with its English meaning:
exercises.target_answer: I would like, you could (polite request), I would do / make, I will speak, I would speak
exercises.meaning: je voudrais (from vouloir), tu pourrais (from pouvoir), je ferais (from faire), je parlerai (infinitive + ai), je parlerais (infinitive + ais)
exercises.explanation: Future ends in -ai (from j'ai); Conditional ends in -ais (from j'avais).

exercises.prompt: Build the conditional 'I would speak' by attaching the imparfait ending -ais to the infinitive parler:
You are ordering red wine at a restaurant. Which is the polite French phrasing?
options: Je voudrais du vin rouge, s'il vous plaît
exercises.target_answer: Je voudrais du vin rouge, s'il vous plaît
exercises.meaning: I would like some red wine, please
exercises.explanation: Je voudrais softens 'I want' into polite 'I would like'.

exercises.idea: I would like to reserve a table for tonight
cues: I would like to reserve a table → Je voudrais réserver une table + for tonight → pour ce soir
idea_parts: polite conditional + infinitive → Je voudrais réserver
exercises.target_answer: Je voudrais réserver une table pour ce soir
exercises.meaning: I would like to reserve a table for tonight
exercises.explanation: Je voudrais pulls the bare infinitive réserver just like je veux.

diagnosis.cue: Use Je voudrais + bare infinitive réserver.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: speak more slowly: parler plus lentement
exercises.explanation: Tu pourrais + infinitive turns a command into a gentle request.
exercises.affirmation: You heard Tu pourrais parler and the -ment adverb lentement.

summary.outcome: Deploy je voudrais, tu pourrais, and je ferais for polite requests and hypotheticals, and recognize the -ai future tense.

use_example.german: Je voudrais vous demander une information.
use_example.english: I would like to ask you for a piece of information.

summary.takeaway: Future stem (/ʁ/) + -ai is 'will'; Future stem (/ʁ/) + -ais is 'would'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2601] Je voudrais): see how The Would-World leads directly into Je voudrais.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'What would you do?' (use Qu'est-ce que tu ferais):
twist.explanation: fer- (future stem of faire) + -ais = tu ferais ('you would do').

foreshadow.line: Having mastered The Would-World, look ahead to Topic 27 (il faut), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 25 (il y a) now pays off directly inside The Would-World: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

voudrais.context_phrase: Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
voudrais.context_translation: I would like a croissant, please.
voudrais.etymology_derivation: Future stem voudr- + imparfait ending -ais = the polite conditional!

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

faire.context_translation: What are you going to do?
faire.etymology_derivation: One French verb covers both 'do' and 'make' (like Spanish hacer and German machen).

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

avoir.etymology_derivation: Latin habēre = have. The H dropped and stayed dropped — French never pronounces its Latin H.

vin.context_translation: I would like some red wine.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → French café. English took the same journey twice: coffee and café.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
